content: The 2010 WHO guidelines on infant feeding in the context of HIV infection recommend exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) for the first six months of life, followed by complementary feeding and continued breastfeeding up to one year of age. This recommendation is made under the condition that either the mother or the infant is receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) to prevent mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV. However, at the time these guidelines were developed, there was limited data on the risk of postnatal HIV transmission in women who were on ART during pregnancy and continued ART after delivery, or in infants who received ART prophylaxis. Over the past five years, additional evidence has emerged from studies and programs that achieved PMTCT postnatally through maternal ART or infant antiretroviral (ARV) prophylaxis. Despite this, the precise risk of HIV transmission and mortality (HIV-free survival) in infants within such programs remains unclear. Furthermore, it is uncertain whether mixed feeding continues to pose a higher risk of HIV transmission compared to exclusive breastfeeding, as was observed in the pre-ART era, or whether effective ARV treatment reduces the risk of transmission to negligible levels regardless of the infant feeding method. In October 2015, WHO convened a Guideline Meeting to review the 2010 guidelines on HIV and infant feeding in light of the increasing use of ART in pregnant and breastfeeding women. One of the key questions addressed was the relationship between infant feeding practices, particularly the duration of breastfeeding, and HIV-free survival in the context of maternal ART. A systematic review was conducted to address the question of HIV-free survival at 12, 18, or 24 months in infants born to women on ART, stratified by infant feeding modality. Data on overall HIV transmission, transmission by six months of age, and HIV-free survival by feeding modality were also presented. A second review separately summarized evidence related to breastfeeding practices during the first six months of life, with HIV transmission at six and 12 months as outcomes. The review included both experimental and observational studies, such as randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, and longitudinal studies. These studies involved HIV-positive mothers receiving ART and their breastfed infants, who may also have received prophylactic ARVs as per the 2010 WHO guidelines. The primary outcomes assessed were HIV-free survival and HIV transmission between birth and 24 months of age. The literature search was conducted using multiple electronic databases, including PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and CINAHL, covering the period from 2005 to 2015. Additional sources included conference abstracts and grey literature. Authors of relevant studies were contacted for additional information when necessary. The search process identified 1,295 citations, of which 156 abstracts were screened. After full-text review, 18 studies were included in the analysis. These studies were conducted in various countries, predominantly in Africa, with one study from India. The studies varied in terms of the timing and duration of maternal ART, breastfeeding recommendations, and practices. The quality of the included studies was assessed using a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). This scale evaluated factors such as the representativeness of the study population, ascertainment of ART and breastfeeding exposure, maternal adherence to ART, and the timing and stratification of HIV-free survival outcomes. The quality of evidence was further evaluated using the GRADE framework, considering study limitations, consistency of results, directness, and publication bias. The studies included in the review reported different types of interventions and outcomes. For example, some studies compared HIV-free survival in children whose mothers received ART versus those who did not, while others compared different ART regimens or durations of exclusive breastfeeding. The pooled estimate of HIV-free survival was calculated using a random-effects meta-analysis, and confidence intervals were provided for most estimates. The findings highlighted the variability in HIV-free survival rates based on the duration of maternal ART and breastfeeding practices. Some studies reported early initiation of ART during pregnancy (14–15 weeks), while others initiated ART later (24–36 weeks). The duration of exclusive breastfeeding ranged from three to six months across studies. The review also presented data on HIV transmission rates at six months and at the end of follow-up, as well as confidence intervals for differences in HIV-free survival between exclusively breastfed and formula-fed infants. In summary, the systematic review provided a comprehensive analysis of HIV-free survival in breastfed infants of HIV-positive mothers on ART, highlighting the impact of maternal ART duration, breastfeeding practices, and other factors on outcomes. The findings informed the revision of WHO guidelines on HIV and infant feeding.
